text:
“I remember,” he began, “a day in the month of March, when you came to see me at my house for the first time. I was asleep. You were almost a child then, or seemed to be, and you showed me a gold bracelet. Yes!... and now I no longer have that house, or at least I must leave it, because there has been a scandal and people avoid greeting me... Do you know? It means that you will have a house, and one more beautiful and richer than mine, since Rafa spends freely. Provided, however, that you do not grow too fat... Rafa, I warn you, abhors women who are too fat. Then I also remember an outing we took together, on the shores of a certain lake... But it was for one night only; perhaps you have lost the memory of it amid so many things.

He watched her, questioned her, intimidated her with his sinister eyes.

“Tell me a little about your life, then!... Have you no voice left?”

His sister asked in a firm, simple tone:

“Why have you come?”

He stared at her for a moment, his eyes gleaming brightly:

“I was passing by,” he replied; “the wall is not high; I felt like paying you a visit.”

“Why have you come?” she repeated once more, in a deeper voice.

“Ah!... Perhaps you thought you would never see me again? Had you already put your heart at peace?”

A wicked and somber anger fleetingly appeared in her, as it did on her brother’s face.

“I have done you no harm,” she said sharply, with complete certainty.

“You?”

“No harm,” she reiterated, more sharply still.

He sprang to his feet, livid, as if to seize her.

“No, do not touch me!” she commanded, shielding herself with both arms. “If you had wanted me, I was yours; you could freely have done with me whatever you pleased... Do not forget it!”

“What are you saying?” he murmured, surprised by these words, struck full force by this truth.

“When I was, as you said, a child, when I came to your house for the first time, and afterward, and always, until the day you fled, you could have done with me whatever you pleased. I would never have taken revenge or complained.”

She too paused, since he was silent, overcome with astonishment.

“But now what are you asking of me?” Loretta added.

“What am I asking of you?... A little clarification, a matter of no consequence: for what reason did you become Rafa’s mistress?”

She turned her eyes irresolutely elsewhere, toward the motionless trees, toward the restless stars, toward the luminous shadow of the cerulean night.

“Answer!”

“I do not know.”

“For love?”

“No.”

“For money?”

“Not that either.”

“Did he perhaps take you by force?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“I do not know, I do not know!...” she said nervously. “Why do you want to torment me?”

“Answer: did you love him? Do you love him?”

“No. I said no.”

She sensed that these words would save her, and repeated once more:

“Neither before nor now; I do not love him.”

And what was more, it was indeed true.

A kind of vertigo passed through the eyes of the man staring at her; a trace, almost already a smile, almost a kiss, rippled across his bitter mouth.

“Then why did you do this?”

“I myself could not tell you,” his sister confessed. “It was madness, a moment of thoughtlessness, something unforeseen and easy, without gravity yet almost necessary... One day I did it, and I cannot even tell you the reason. Perhaps because you had tormented me so much, perhaps because I made the mistake of going up a staircase... I do not know, I do not know!”

And now she was no longer afraid of him; she spoke to him almost gently, her lovely color returning to her blooming cheeks, passing a ringed hand over her white temple and smoothing her hair with a habitual gesture of hers.

“And I?” her brother murmured after remaining silent.

“You?”

“Yes, Lora, I, who loved you with such anguish, I, who fled desperately so as not to hurt you?...”

She hesitated a little, then said:

“You did not want me... you did not want me even when I wept over it, and so...”

In the terrible simplicity of these words she gathered together the entire logic of her little woman’s heart; she solved her little feminine enigma, in which the maddest love had, at bottom, been nothing but a murky curiosity. She could go no further; the whole story of her great sin ended in this small reflection: “You did not want me, and so...”

And he lowered his face, then began rapping his knuckles on the little wicker table, which rocked.

“So,” he said, bitterly and mockingly, “you simply needed someone to lay you down forcefully, with your shoulders upon a cushion, someone to make you finally utter that little cry... Who that person was mattered little. I had tormented you greatly... did you say tormented?... very well, so be it! But in any case you chose a rich man, to sweeten the pains of martyrdom; in exchange you wanted a few dresses, a few jewels, a house that will end up becoming yours... there, and you have all of that!”

“What I wanted,” she explained, “was to choose for myself a life different from the one I was leading: nothing else. Perhaps I was mistaken as well.”

He stared at her again with a doubtful look, then changed his line of thought:

“Why are you alone this evening?”

“I am alone many times,” she replied.

They fell silent; a long silence ruled over their uneasiness. He waited for her to speak; she was waiting for his words. And they studied each other attentively; each sought to read the other’s heart.

“So,” he resumed after that pause, “so you have nothing to say to me?”

“Yes, many things... but I am afraid of you.”

“And you are right,” her brother said. “I have reached that hour when nothing and no one is respected any longer, when an entire story is approaching its final peril. Nevertheless, I will listen to you, if you have something to tell me, and I still listen to you with kindness, Lora, because I am still the same... I repeat: still the same.”

And in these last words he put into his voice a tone as tender as a caress.

“Sit down,” he added; “come closer to me.”

“No!” she said twice, “no.”

“Are you afraid?”

She did not answer; but it seemed that anguish, pity, a compassion almost bordering on revulsion, stifled her soul in that refusal.

On the threshold of the half-dark room, Lazzara’s figure appeared, full of hesitation, yet with the air of being there to bring her aid.

The man turned toward her with a sudden movement:

“What do you want?” he lashed out.

The girl did not answer; her frightened eyes moved from one to the other, as if trying to guess.

But Loretta said to her:

“Do not be afraid, Lazzara. Go up to your room and sleep. My brother will leave shortly.”

“Your brother, madam?...” the girl uttered, unable to believe herself in her amazement.

“Go up and sleep, Lazzara,” Lora commanded curtly.

She withdrew in small steps, silent, and disappeared into the darkness. A little later, from within the thickness of the ancient wall, there burst forth the sound of running water, which in the resonance of the night filled the deep house with sound. Then it ceased: the lofty rooms fell asleep.
